chapter_theme: Lovesick Gunamalai, praising a woman's restraint yet thinking of the palmyra horse, sends her parrot to Civakan, who has painted her portrait and is embracing it; his wife Gandharvadattai comes upon the picture, sees through his excuse, scorns his appeasing words and leaves in a sulk, and the parrot, which waited hidden, comes down to his hand.

cast.role: the merchant's daughter whom Civakan saved from the elephant, now in love with him
Gunamalai's parrot, sent as her messenger
the hero, already married to Gandharvadattai
Civakan's wife, won at the vina contest

998.reading: Gunamalai says her eyes have lost their brightness, her bangles slip, and her heart cries out like a wound; a woman, though desire burns her, does not go forward, and nothing surpasses womanhood.

claims.claim: a woman, however desire burns her, does not make the first advance

998.nuance: She praises the very restraint that is hurting her; the next verse shows how close it comes to breaking. The thought is the Kural's on women and the palmyra horse (1137) in other words, not a verbal echo.

999.reading: As her longing rises like the great sea, the girl with spear-like eyes thinks of riding the palmyra-stem horse with its hanging leaves.
999.event: Gunamalai, overcome by longing, considers riding the madal.
999.nuance: The madal is a man's public threat; a heroine only thinking of it shows desire pressing past the rule she has just praised. She thinks of it but turns to the parrot instead.

1000.reading: Gunamalai begs her red-beaked parrot, whom she calls her only refuge, to tell her how she may live, and the parrot tells her not to waste away and to say without shame whom in the land she wants.
1000.event: Gunamalai asks her parrot for help, and the parrot asks her to name the man.
1000.nuance: The closing என்றதே, a neuter verb, gives lines 3 and 4 to the parrot; the division of the speeches is my reading.

1001.reading: They say that she, matchless in radiance and grace even against the goddess on the lotus, helpless in heady desire, told her parrot her message and sent it as her envoy.
1001.event: Gunamalai sends her parrot as messenger to Civakan.

1002.reading: With her modesty, her family and her good name set beneath her longing, the dear green parrot flew through the sky to find the master of the vina.
1002.event: The parrot flies off to find Civakan.
1002.nuance: Sending a go-between is itself counted as a loss of நாண், family standing and name: the price of the message is set before the message arrives.

1003.reading: Civakan blended and purified many coloured gems and painted on cloth the girl with the tilaka brow, as she was in look and trembling when she stood terrified before the rutting elephant.
1003.event: Civakan paints Gunamalai's portrait on cloth as she stood before the elephant.
1003.nuance: He paints her not at ease but at the moment of terror: the danger that brought them together is the image he keeps.

1004.reading: Gazing and gazing at the painting, he strokes its slipping garment, falling hair, garland and the pearls on her young breasts, praises it, and clasps it to his shoulders.
1004.event: Civakan caresses and embraces the portrait.

1005.reading: Civakan says that the jewelled girdle on her broad hips, the ornaments on her breasts and the anklets on her lotus feet must all have done penance to be worn by her.

claims.claim: a fortunate place is the fruit of penance once performed

1005.nuance: The verb நோற்ற, repeated three times, turns the language of the vow into a lover's compliment; the fancy assumes that good fortune is earned by austerity.

1006.reading: While the prince lamented thus over her grace, the parrot of the girl of tormenting speech saw with delight Tattai, the prince's beloved, arriving.
1006.event: As Civakan laments, the parrot sees Gandharvadattai approaching.
1006.nuance: The line puns on தத்தை, parrot and Gandharvadattai's short name: the parrot sees Tattai. The sense of மன்னணங் குறலொடு is doubtful.

1007.reading: On her hips, wide as a dancing snake's hood, the fine cloth wrapped over her girdle looked as if pale smoke of incense had gathered and curled about it.

1008.reading: The bright strands of pearl hanging over the tips of her rising breasts looked like young crescent moons drawn on a golden casket.

1009.reading: With an earring arching its light on one side and an ear-roll flashing on the other, the beauty of her face was like a full round moon.

1010.reading: The fine gold thread drawn through the dark hair at her forehead shone like lightning curved through a dark sky.
1010.nuance: Which ornament நாணிற of line 3 names is not certain from the line alone.

1011.reading: The jasmine garland trailing from her fragrant hair-knot looked like a koel bending on a swaying flowering creeper.

1012.reading: The parrot wonders who this wide-eyed woman can be, who walks with anklets and girdle chiming like a golden flowering creeper that has learned to walk while bees hum on it.

1013.reading: Saying that whoever she is, it will not go near on its errand until she has done what she came for and gone, the green parrot settles in a flowering champak.
1013.event: The parrot waits hidden in a champak tree.
1013.nuance: The envoy keeps the go-between's rule of secrecy: the message is for him alone.

1014.reading: The honey-eyed woman, gold anklet-bells tinkling as she walked, came up to the man of the fierce spear, saw, and looked at him in a sulk.
1014.event: Gandharvadattai comes upon Civakan with the portrait and sulks.

1015.reading: Asked what the figure was, he called it a yakshi, and she answers that this is something new: since his garment and hair hang loose and that garlanded one so moves his mind, she must indeed be an iyakki.
1015.event: Civakan passes the portrait off as a yakshi, and Gandharvadattai turns the word against him.
1015.nuance: The retort puns on இயக்கி, a yakshi and 'one who sets in motion'. Who asks and who answers in line 1 is my reading.

1016.reading: Sweat beaded on her face like pearls on a rising moon, her brows bent like a bow, and her eyes reddened like a cluster of water lilies.

1017.reading: Civakan pleads with her not to draw out her sulk: for him, a wretch, they are one life in two bodies, and would a swan that delighted in the flowering Ganges go near the white sand of a seep-well?
1017.nuance: The Ganges and the well rank the two women: to soothe the wife he belittles the girl he has just embraced in paint.

1018.reading: Looking at the painted figure, she who flares at other women even by name felt her sulk toward her loving husband blaze like fire with ghee poured on it.
1018.event: Gandharvadattai's anger grows as she looks at the portrait.

1019.reading: Trembling like a creeper in her anger, anklets and girdle chiming, she set her flower-feet upon his garlanded head, turned with her earrings flashing, scattered her flowers and left.
1019.nuance: Line 3 seems to have him bow and her feet touch his head; the gesture and who makes it are not plain.

1020.reading: When his wife had gone with angry words, the parrot, saying that now there was no one else and it would come out, mixed sweet words and flew to the young man's feet.
1020.event: The parrot comes down to Civakan once Gandharvadattai has gone.

1021.reading: The parrot hails his anklet-feet and wishes him long life; he answers 'welcome, friend, come here', and the master of the yazh holds out his hand, his gem rings flashing.
1021.event: Civakan welcomes the parrot onto his hand.
1021.nuance: The welcome is the borrowed word சுவாகதம், svāgatam, a courtly greeting.

links.note: The Kural praises womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and does not ride the palmyra horse; Gunamalai, with longing like the sea, considers riding it.
links.teaches: The epic shows the couplet's praised restraint from inside, as a near thing: the heroine reaches the very thought of the madal before turning to a go-between, so the Kural's 'does not ride' names a line held under pressure, not an absence of the wish.

gains.a: Gunamalai's thought of the madal gains its measure: it is the one act the ethical tradition says a woman forgoes
gains.b: the couplet's abstract womanhood gains a woman who voices its praise of herself (998) and then wavers, which a gnomic line cannot show

links.note: The Kural's wife takes offence even at his adoring gaze, asking whom he is thinking of; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes at a portrait of another woman painted by her husband.
links.teaches: The Kural's comedy of jealousy depends on the husband's innocence, and the epic removes it: here the suspected other woman is real and painted by his own hand, so the sulk is no longer love's game but a just grievance.

gains.a: Gandharvadattai's flare is placed in a known type, the wife of the pulavi nunukkam who reads every look as a rival
gains.b: the couplet's baseless suspicion is set against a case where suspicion is right, showing how much its charm rests on there being no rival

links.note: The Kural's lover says his bond with the girl is that of body and life; Civakan tells his sulking wife they are one life in two bodies.
links.teaches: Spoken with another woman's portrait still in his arms, the claim of a single life becomes an appeasing formula, so the Cintamani shows the Kural's declaration of union put to use in a marriage that is about to take a second wife.

gains.a: Civakan's line gains the weight of the classic declaration it reworks, which makes its hollowness here visible
gains.b: the couplet, spoken in first love, gains a later setting that tests whether the claim survives a rival

links.note: Gunamalai stood before the charging elephant looking about with doe eyes and trembling like lightning; Civakan paints exactly her look and her trembling.
links.teaches: The lover's image of the beloved is the instant of her mortal fear, so what he desires and keeps is the moment he saved her, and the rescue becomes the ground of the love.

links.note: Gunamalai fears she has no way to live, like little people who have done no tapas; Civakan says her very ornaments did penance to be on her.
links.teaches: Apart and unknown to each other, both lovers reach for the language of penance: she counts herself among those without its merit, while he grants its merit even to her jewels, so the same idea marks her despair and his worship.

links.note: Civakan praised Gunamalai so that even her girdle and anklets had done penance; to his wife he calls her the sand of a seep-well beside the Ganges.
links.teaches: Within a few verses the hero ranks the same woman as worthy of the jewels' penance and as a puddle beside his wife, so the poem lets the reader see his words to each woman fitted to the listener.

links.note: Gunamalai wasted like a garland in a ghee-fed flame; Gandharvadattai's sulk blazes like fire with ghee poured on it.
links.teaches: One simile serves both women: the fire that consumed the girl's longing now feeds the wife's jealousy, so the poem sets the two women's passions, love and anger, burning from the same man.

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken

source_issues: 998 line 3: வெண்ணில் is doubtful (perhaps எண்ணில்); the reading of the line is uncertain.
1000 line 3: நைய னங்கையிற் நாட்டகத் shows an irregular junction (ற் before ந); perhaps நையல் நங்கை இந்நாட்டகத்து.
1012 line 2: பூங்கெடி is probably a misprint for பூங்கொடி.
1014 line 3: வேலினாற் கண்டு is odd as written; the sense needs the spear-bearer as object of கண்டு.
